patient.name: Niamh Brennan
patient.complaint: Took 60 aspirin tablets 50 minutes ago; ringing in her ears and breathing fast

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?' with an ABG and electrolytes: decide acidosis or alkalosis from pH, then whether CO2 or HCO3- is driving it, then calculate the anion gap.

points: Breathing fast and deep; feels light-headed.

steps.lead: Niamh's blood pH is held between **7.35 and 7.45**. Aspirin can push it either way, so read the gas systematically.

steps.title: ABG on arrival (breathing air)
steps.text: High pH with a **low CO2**: the CO2 explains the pH, so it is respiratory.

steps.lead: Early aspirin overdose drives Niamh to **hyperventilate**: a **respiratory alkalosis**, the same pattern as a panic attack, PE or high altitude.

steps.title: Reading any gas in four steps
nodes: CO2: does it explain the pH? → respiratory
HCO3-: does it explain the pH? → metabolic
Is the other value moving to compensate?
Metabolic acidosis? → calculate the anion gap
steps.caption: Never stop at pH: a fully compensated disorder can have a normal pH.

steps.lead: Niamh's only clue was her **breathing pattern**. Interpreting **CO2 and HCO3-** together is what names the disorder.

points: Six hours later she is drowsy and vomiting.

steps.title: Repeat ABG at 6 hours
steps.text: Now low pH and low HCO3-: **metabolic acidosis**, with low CO2 as respiratory compensation.

steps.lead: Niamh's gap is (140 + 4) − (12 + 102) = **30**: raised. **S**alicylates is the last letter of MUDPILES.

steps.q: Which pattern does Niamh's 6 hour gas show?
steps.r: Low pH and HCO3-, gap of **30**. Her CO2 is low (compensation), so there is no respiratory acidosis.

visual.title: Niamh's anion gap
visual.label: Niamh 30
visual.caption: Above 20: extra unmeasured acid (here salicylate and lactate).

steps.lead: Niamh breathes fast. A **COPD** patient or someone after a **heroin** overdose does the opposite: CO2 builds up and pH falls.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' (an ABG) or a calculation, such as the anion gap from the electrolytes given.

steps.q: Which test names Niamh's acid-base disorder?
steps.r: The **ABG** gives pH, PaCO2 and HCO3- together, which is what you need to classify the disorder.

steps.lead: Niamh's two **ABGs** told the story: alkalosis at 50 minutes, acidosis at 6 hours.

visual.title: Arterial pH
visual.label: Niamh 7.29 at 6 h
visual.caption: Below 7.35 confirms acidosis. Her first gas, 7.51, sat in the alkalosis band.

steps.lead: With the pattern known, Niamh needs **targeted tests**: salicylate and paracetamol levels, U&Es, glucose and lactate.

steps.title: Targeted bloods
steps.text: A salicylate over 500 mg/L is **significant toxicity**. Always check paracetamol in any overdose.
Anion gap = (Na + K) − (HCO3- + Cl). Normal **10–20 mmol/L**. Above 20 means unmeasured acid: think MUDPILES.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': treat the cause. Know the specific ones: activated charcoal for aspirin, fomepizole for ethylene glycol, NIV for COPD, insulin for DKA.

steps.lead: Niamh's acid-base problem is fixed by treating its **cause**, the salicylate. The same rule gives insulin in DKA and NIV in COPD.

steps.q: Niamh arrived 50 minutes after taking the tablets. What is the first step?
steps.r: **Activated charcoal** decontaminates the gut, ideally within an hour. Bicarbonate comes later for significant toxicity.

steps.lead: Niamh gets **charcoal** first. Her level of 650 mg/L then justifies **IV sodium bicarbonate** to alkalinise the urine and speed elimination.

steps.title: Treat the cause
nodes: COPD with high CO2 → controlled oxygen and NIV
Aspirin → charcoal, then bicarbonate if severe
steps.caption: There is no single 'acidosis drug': the answer is always the cause's treatment.

visual.title: Niamh on treatment
visual.caption: Alkalosis first, then acidosis at 6 hours. Treating the salicylate (bicarbonate from 6 h) brings pH back to normal.

steps.lead: Niamh needs **IV fluids** and monitoring. If she became comatose or her pH kept falling, she would need **ICU** (and dialysis for salicylate).
The **anion gap** and **MUDPILES** guided Niamh's work-up and pointed straight at the salicylate.

steps.text: A rebreathing bag is not for aspirin overdose. It is only for severe **anxiety** hyperventilation, after breathing techniques fail.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why a patient hyperventilates in metabolic acidosis, why vomiting causes alkalosis, or which mechanism produces a normal or raised anion gap.

steps.lead: Niamh's buffer is **bicarbonate**: her lungs control CO2 within minutes; her kidneys control HCO3- and H+ over days.

steps.title: The bicarbonate buffer
nodes: Lungs adjust CO2; kidneys adjust HCO3-
pH follows the HCO3- : CO2 ratio

steps.lead: Salicylate and lactate are **added acid**, so Niamh's gap rose. Losing bicarbonate in diarrhoea would leave the gap **normal**.
Niamh's deep breathing at 6 hours is **compensation**: blowing off CO2 to drag pH back up, like Kussmaul breathing in DKA.

steps.q: Why did Niamh breathe fast within an hour of the overdose?
o: Direct stimulation of the respiratory centre
Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis
steps.r: Salicylate **directly stimulates the respiratory centre** early, causing a primary respiratory alkalosis. Compensation came later.

steps.lead: Niamh blew off too much CO2 (**alveolar hyperventilation**). Opioids or COPD cause the reverse: **hypoventilation** and CO2 retention.
Niamh vomited a little, but prolonged vomiting would lose **HCl** and volume, so the kidneys hold bicarbonate: **metabolic alkalosis**.

visual.title: Niamh's PaCO2 against her HCO3-
visual.caption: Early: CO2 falls first (primary). At 6 h: HCO3- falls (primary), CO2 stays low (compensation).

mcq.q: What is the normal range of arterial pH?
mcq.r: **7.35–7.45**: below is acidosis, above is alkalosis.

mcq.q: Most common cause of respiratory acidosis?
Most common cause of respiratory alkalosis?
Severe prolonged vomiting causes which disorder?
mcq.r: Loss of gastric HCl: **hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis**.

mcq.q: Severe diarrhoea (e.g. Crohn's) gives which acidosis?
mcq.r: Bicarbonate loss: **normal anion gap**, with hypokalaemia.

mcq.q: What is the normal anion gap?
Gold-standard test for an acid-base disorder?
mcq.r: The **ABG** gives pH, PaCO2 and HCO3- together.
**Activated charcoal**; bicarbonate is for significant toxicity.

mcq.q: Why does a patient in metabolic acidosis hyperventilate?
o: To blow off CO2 and raise pH
mcq.r: Respiratory **compensation**: lowering CO2 pushes pH back up.

technique.stem: A 22 year old woman has a 3 day history of profuse watery diarrhoea from a flare of Crohn's disease. She feels weak and dizzy. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute.
technique.q: What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?

steps.x: An acid-base question: pH, then CO2 or HCO3-, then the gap.
Diarrhoea loses bicarbonate. pH 7.28 and HCO3- 14: **metabolic acidosis**; low CO2 is compensation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gap = (138 + 3) − (14 + 114) = **13**: normal. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with low K.

elim: That is vomiting; here pH is low and chloride high.
The gap is 13, inside 10–20.
CO2 is low, not high.
pH is low, so it is an acidosis.

steps.x: **B. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.** Diarrhoea loses HCO3-; the gap stays normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

technique.stem: A 70 year old man with COPD has a 2 day history of increasing breathlessness and green sputum. He is drowsy. He is on 28% oxygen via a Venturi mask. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89%. He has had nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium and oral prednisolone.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Repeat nebulisers and review in 4 hours

steps.x: Next step: name the disorder, then treat its cause.

clues: nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium and oral prednisolone
steps.x: pH 7.26, CO2 8.9: **respiratory acidosis** (HCO3- 30 is partial renal compensation). Medical therapy already given.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 5 day history of persistent vomiting from hyperemesis. She is dizzy on standing. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her acid-base disturbance?
o: Loss of bicarbonate in the stool

steps.x: A mechanism question: classify the gas, then explain it.
High pH and HCO3-, low chloride: **hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis**. Raised CO2 is compensation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Vomiting loses **gastric HCl**; volume depletion then makes the kidneys retain bicarbonate.

elim: Would cause acidosis, not alkalosis.
CO2 would be low; here it is high.
Diarrhoea causes normal gap acidosis.
Causes acidosis (uraemia).

steps.x: **D. Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid.** Vomiting = HCl loss = hypochloraemic alkalosis.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman has sudden breathlessness, tingling around her mouth and in her fingers after an argument. She feels her heart pounding. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 100% breathing air.
practice.q: What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
practice.e: High pH, low CO2, high oxygen and normal HCO3-: acute uncompensated respiratory alkalosis from anxiety hyperventilation. Renal compensation takes days, so HCO3- is still normal.

steps.x: Classify the gas: pH, then which value explains it.
pH 7.54 (alkalosis) with CO2 2.8 (low) and normal HCO3-.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute **respiratory alkalosis** from hyperventilation (the commonest cause).

elim: pH is high, not low.
HCO3- is normal; the CO2 explains the pH.
CO2 is low and pH high.
HCO3- has not fallen: no compensation yet (acute).

steps.x: **D. Respiratory alkalosis.** Low CO2, high pH, normal HCO3- = acute.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with COPD has a 3 day history of increasing breathlessness and purulent sputum. He is drowsy. His pulse rate is 100 bpm, BP 150/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air.
practice.q: What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
o: Respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation
practice.e: Low pH with high CO2 is respiratory acidosis; the raised HCO3- is chronic renal compensation in COPD, but pH is still low, so compensation is partial.

steps.x: Classify the gas: does CO2 or HCO3- explain the low pH?
pH 7.27, CO2 9.2 (high): respiratory acidosis. HCO3- 31 is high, which opposes the acidosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation** (acute on chronic).

elim: HCO3- is high, not low.
pH is low, so the primary problem is acidosis.
Needs a low HCO3-; it is raised.
CO2 is high.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation.** COPD is the classic cause.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man is brought in after being found collapsed with slurred speech, smelling of alcohol. His friend says he drank screenwash from the garage. His pulse rate is 112 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute.
practice.q: What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
practice.e: Low pH and HCO3- with a gap of (141 + 4.8) − (7 + 103) ≈ 36: a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis from ethylene glycol or methanol. Low CO2 is compensation.

steps.x: Classify, then calculate the gap.
Screenwash contains **methanol or ethylene glycol** (M and E of MUDPILES). Normal glucose excludes DKA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: pH 7.15, HCO3- 7; gap about **36**: raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.

elim: pH is low.
The gap is about 36.
CO2 is low (compensation), not high.
pH is low.

steps.x: **C. Raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.** Toxic alcohols are MUDPILES causes.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and a syringe beside him. His pulse rate is 58 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 6 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82% breathing air.
practice.q: What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?

Opioid overdose, RR 6: **hypoventilation** retains CO2.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has recurrent renal stones and muscle weakness. She has no diarrhoea or vomiting and takes no medicines. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her acid-base disturbance?
practice.e: Normal anion gap (about 12), hyperchloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic acidosis with stones and an inappropriately alkaline urine is type 1 RTA. Addison's gives a normal gap but high potassium.

Gap = (139 + 2.9) − (15 + 115) ≈ 12: **normal gap**, high chloride, low potassium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No diarrhoea, stones, alkaline urine: **type 1 renal tubular acidosis**.

elim: Normal gap too, but causes hyperkalaemia.
Raised gap from ketones.
Raised gap.
Raised gap, with an overdose history.

steps.x: **D. Renal tubular acidosis type 1.** Normal gap + low K + no diarrhoea = RTA 1.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman takes chlortalidone for hypertension. She has felt tired with muscle cramps for 2 weeks. She has no vomiting. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.

pH 7.49 and HCO3- 33: **metabolic alkalosis**. CO2 6.3 is raised to compensate.

elim: pH is high.
pH would be low or normal; here it is high.
CO2 is high, not low.
CO2 would be low and HCO3- low.

steps.x: **B. Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.** Thiazides cause metabolic alkalosis.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has a 2 day history of vomiting and abdominal pain. He is drowsy and breathing deeply. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. A venous sample is available.

glossary.acidosis: A process lowering blood pH below 7.35.
glossary.alkalosis: A process raising blood pH above 7.45.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: measures pH, PaO2, PaCO2 and bicarbonate in arterial blood.
glossary.VBG: Venous blood gas: gives pH and bicarbonate reliably, but not oxygen.
glossary.PaCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood; normal 4.7–6.0 kPa.
glossary.PaO2: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood; normal 11–13 kPa on air.
glossary.HCO3-: Bicarbonate, the main blood buffer base; normal 22–26 mmol/L.
glossary.bicarbonate buffer: The CO2, carbonic acid and bicarbonate system that resists changes in pH.
glossary.compensation: A change in the other system (lungs or kidneys) that pushes pH back towards normal.
glossary.anion gap: (Na + K) − (HCO3- + Cl); a raised value means unmeasured acid such as ketones or lactate.
glossary.unmeasured anions: Negative ions not included in routine tests, such as lactate, ketones and toxin acids.
glossary.MUDPILES: Mnemonic for raised anion gap acidosis: methanol, uraemia, DKA, paracetamol, iron, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates.
glossary.uraemia: Build-up of urea and other waste products from kidney failure.
glossary.lactic acidosis: Acidosis from lactate, usually from poor tissue perfusion (sepsis, ischaemia).
glossary.DKA: Diabetic ketoacidosis: hyperglycaemia, ketones and metabolic acidosis from insulin deficiency.
glossary.ketoacidosis: Acidosis caused by ketone bodies, as in DKA or alcoholic ketoacidosis.
glossary.alcoholic ketoacidosis: Ketoacidosis after heavy drinking and starvation, with a normal or low glucose.
glossary.renal tubular acidosis: Failure of the kidney tubules to excrete acid or keep bicarbonate, giving a normal gap acidosis.
glossary.hyperchloraemic: With a raised blood chloride, typical of normal anion gap acidosis.
glossary.hypochloraemic: With a low blood chloride, typical of vomiting.
glossary.villous adenoma: A colonic polyp that can secrete large amounts of fluid and potassium.
glossary.chlortalidone: A thiazide-like diuretic that can cause metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia.
glossary.thiazides: Diuretics acting on the distal tubule; cause hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
glossary.hyperventilation: Breathing more than needed, which lowers CO2 and raises pH.
glossary.hypoventilation: Breathing too little, which raises CO2 and lowers pH.
glossary.Kussmaul breathing: Deep, laboured breathing that blows off CO2 to compensate for metabolic acidosis.
glossary.salicylate: Aspirin and related drugs; overdose causes respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis.
glossary.tinnitus: Ringing in the ears; an early sign of salicylate toxicity.
glossary.activated charcoal: Oral adsorbent that binds drugs in the gut; best within an hour of ingestion.
glossary.sodium bicarbonate: IV alkali used in salicylate poisoning to alkalinise urine and speed excretion.
glossary.fomepizole: Antidote for ethylene glycol and methanol; blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.
glossary.ethylene glycol: Toxic alcohol in antifreeze; causes raised anion gap acidosis and kidney injury.
glossary.methanol: Toxic alcohol in screenwash; causes raised anion gap acidosis and blindness.
glossary.osmolal gap: Measured minus calculated osmolality; raised by toxic alcohols.
glossary.NIV: Non-invasive ventilation: mask ventilation that helps blow off CO2 in respiratory acidosis.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; the most important cause of respiratory acidosis.
glossary.thiamine: Vitamin B1; given before glucose in alcohol-related illness to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
glossary.Addison's disease: Primary adrenal insufficiency; can cause normal gap acidosis with hyperkalaemia.
glossary.metformin: Oral diabetes drug that rarely causes lactic acidosis, especially in renal failure.
